title: VR experience optimisation

sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOC's course on Foundations for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
We are discussing a topic related to the optimization of experience.
In particular, we are talking about the optimization of VR navigation experience.
So, we will continue our discussion on that topic in this part of the lecture as well.

Earlier, we talked about one model for a realistic walking experience; that is, we are assuming that we are having a system-controlled VR tour where user movements and navigation will be controlled by the system.
Now, to provide the user a natural walking experience, we have seen a model for that; we can use that model to provide the user the natural walking experience.
Now, that model is supposed to display a visual speed, or the optic flow, which is the rate at which the scenes change in the virtual world, so that the user gets the perception of movement.
Now, that visual speed is supposed to be provided by the walking model, which matches the user's instantaneous walking speed.
Rather, we should say the perceived instantaneous walking speed.
So that is the model.
Now, that model itself does not provide anything related to experience optimization.
It can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.
Now, in this lecture, what we are going to do is basically see the use of the model, and with that model, how we can go for an optimization approach where we will try to optimize for cyber sickness.
Also, it may be noted that in this lecture, we are going to talk about one such approach.
There are many other approaches.
In a subsequent part of the lecture, we will talk about another approach as well.
Now, this approach we can broadly term as addressing the cyber sickness concern, that is, optimizing cyber sickness by controlling the exposure duration.
So, earlier we talked about one of the factors of cyber sickness being the duration of exposure in the virtual world.
So here, our objective would be to try to optimize the exposure duration so that cyber sickness can be optimized.
Details about this can be found at the reference mentioned at the end of the overall lecture, reference number 4.
We will point out the relevant reference when we reach the end of the lecture.
Now, if you can recollect, cyber sickness is correlated to the exposure duration in a VR environment, as we have repeatedly seen in our discussions on cyber sickness.
Now, the degree of the symptoms rises proportionally with the VR session duration.
The more the duration is, the more the exposure is, the more severe the symptoms will be.
So, clearly, shorter duration exposure, if possible, can help in getting rid of the cyber sickness problem or at least can help in minimizing the onset of cyber sickness.
So, that is the basic assumption on which our approach will be built.

Now, the duration of exposure to cyber sickness depends on several factors, such as the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, or the travelling time, interaction time, such as interaction with objects, such as inspection, selection, and manipulation of objects.
So, there are several factors.
The size of the virtual world, let us see how it affects.
Now, a VR environment can be very small, such as a room, or very large, like a city, or sometimes even larger, such as the Majuli Island that we talked about in our case study.
For large or larger VR systems or environments, it is quite natural to have a longer duration of VR exposure because the user needs to cover a larger geographical area.
Now, we can reduce the exposure time if we can control the speed of movement, the speed of navigation.
This is quite obvious: the higher the speed is, the lower will be the time to travel and explore the entire geographical area.
So, duration and travel speed are related, intimately related.
Now, duration can be adjusted by adjusting the virtual travel speed, which is quite obvious.
So, higher speed effectively refers to a shorter duration of exposure in the virtual world.
However, to provide a realistic walking experience, we cannot modify the speed arbitrarily.
So, Teleportation-type movement, of course, would be the best choice.
There, the speed is the maximum, so instantaneous movement occurs between two points, so then the overall duration can be reduced.
However, that may not always be a good way to approach the problem because teleportation is not a natural movement.
Sometimes we look for naturalness.
In that case, such type of movement or any arbitrary speed imposed on the user while navigating in the virtual world may not be a good idea.
There can be other ways to control the duration, such as manipulation of the terrain or the or the size of the world.
By adjusting the distances between the points of interest in the terrain, by adjusting the terrain of course, we can reduce the travel time and subsequently reduce the exposure time.
But the problem here is that it excludes users from getting an idea about the size of the real space.
So, this is similar to having a teleportation-type movement.
If we arbitrarily change the terrain shape, then the user will not get the true feel of the terrain.
So, that will hamper the user's ability to build a mental map, which in effect can hamper the user's ability to do the wayfinding activities in the virtual world.
To get some idea on this mental map, please refer to our earlier lecture on wayfinding, where we talked about the need for a mental map and how it helps in wayfinding.
In the case of a purely system-automated or system-controlled tool, users do not interact.
So, there is no scope for the user to interactively change anything.
So, in that case, we can ignore the interaction time, that is, the time required to interact with the virtual objects.
In such a scenario, when we are talking of an entirely system-controlled VR tool, the interaction time can be ignored.
However, we are concerned with semi-interactive tours.
That means we are not totally disregarding interactions.
Users can still interact with objects after a navigation task is complete.

So, there the travel will be automatic, system-controlled, but the interactions can happen on a limited scale only at the points of interest, or a small set of objects, all objects that are present in the virtual environment.
Only with those objects are users allowed to interact in the virtual world.
With other objects, users cannot interact.
So, if such a scenario is assumed, then we can call it a semi-interactive tour: interaction with POIs and navigation by system control.
So, the same idea we have used while formulating the natural walking speed model.

So, you can refer to that part of the lecture, the previous lecture, to get some idea on this assumption: that movement from one point to another is controlled by the system tool, whereas at specific chosen points called points of interest, users can interact with those.
So, our objective is to deal with semi-interactive system control tools and thereby reduce the duration of exposure to the virtual world.

Now, this idea of a semi-interactive tour and appropriate time of interaction—so there is a limit on the time of interaction—can be utilized to optimize the duration of exposure in a virtual tour in either of two ways.

parts.objective: Explain an approach to optimize VR experience by controlling exposure duration to address cyber sickness

key_points.text: The foundational walking model used to enhance presence (by displaying optic flow) does not itself optimize the user experience.
The proposed optimization approach focuses on mitigating cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.
Cyber sickness symptoms rise proportionally with the duration of the VR session.
Minimizing cyber sickness can be achieved, or at least helped, by reducing the duration of exposure.

terms.name: Realistic walking experience
terms.definition: Realistic walking experience is a type of VR tour in which the system controls the user's movements and navigation.

terms.name: System-controlled VR tour
terms.definition: System-controlled VR tour is a VR tour where the system controls the user's movements and navigation rather than the user.

terms.name: Natural walking experience
terms.definition: Natural walking experience is a VR experience that provides the user with a visual speed, or optic flow, corresponding to their perceived instantaneous walking speed.

terms.name: Optic flow
terms.definition: Optic flow is the visual speed—the rate at which scenes in a virtual world change—which creates the perception of movement for the user.

terms.name: Presence
terms.definition: Presence in the virtual world is something that the walking model can be used to enhance.

terms.name: Cyber sickness
terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition related to exposure in a VR environment, where the degree of symptoms increases proportionally with the duration of the VR session.

terms.name: Exposure duration
terms.definition: Exposure duration is the amount of time spent in the virtual world, which is a factor correlated to cyber sickness. Optimizing this duration is an approach to minimizing cyber sickness.

parts.objective: Analyze how world size, travel speed, and movement choices influence the duration of VR exposure and cyber sickness

key_points.text: The duration of exposure to cyber sickness depends on factors like virtual world size, travelling speed, and interaction time.
For larger VR environments, longer exposure duration is natural because the user must cover a greater geographical area.
Increasing the speed of movement reduces the travel time, thereby shortening the overall duration of VR exposure.
Key point: "While teleportation reduces exposure duration through instantaneous movement, arbitrary changes to terrain shape can hamper a user's ability to build a mental map." (cited sentences)

terms.name: Size of the virtual world
terms.definition: The size of the virtual world refers to the geographical scale of the environment, which can range from very small, like a room, to very large, such as a city.

terms.name: Virtual travel speed
terms.definition: Virtual travel speed is a factor in the virtual world that can be adjusted; a higher speed effectively results in a shorter duration of exposure.

terms.name: Teleportation-type movement
terms.definition: Teleportation-type movement is a method of navigation where instantaneous movement occurs between two points, which allows for a reduction in overall exposure duration.

terms.name: Mental map
terms.definition: A mental map is something a user builds to facilitate wayfinding activities in the virtual world.

parts.objective: Define and analyze semi-interactive tours where navigation is system-controlled but interaction is limited

key_points.text: In purely system-automated tools, user interaction is nonexistent, allowing the interaction time to be ignored.-
Semi-interactive tours allow for automatic, system-controlled travel while permitting limited user interactions.-
In a semi-interactive tour, users can only interact with a small set of designated Points of Interest (POIs).-
The primary objective is to study semi-interactive system control tools to reduce the required duration of virtual world exposure.

terms.name: System-controlled tool
terms.definition: A purely system-controlled tool is a system where users do not interact, meaning there is no scope for the user to change anything.

terms.name: Entirely system-controlled VR tool
terms.definition: An entirely system-controlled VR tool is a tool where users do not interact and there is no scope to interactively change anything. In such a scenario, the interaction time can be ignored because the system controls the experience.

terms.name: Semi-interactive tour
terms.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a system where the navigation is automatic and controlled by the system, but users can still interact with limited objects.

parts.objective: Compare two strategies for optimizing VR tour exposure duration using predetermined time constraints

key_points.text: Interaction time at points of interest (POIs) can be limited by estimating the maximum required time for a typical user.
VR tour optimization can be approached in two ways using semi-interactive tours based on time limits.
The first optimization problem seeks an optimum path to experience all POIs while minimizing the total time required for navigation and interaction.
The second optimization problem seeks an optimum path to experience the maximum possible number of POIs within a given fixed time.
Optimizing the duration of exposure in VR is intended to optimize the onset and prevalence of cyber sickness.

terms.name: Point of interest
terms.definition: A point of interest is a location within a virtual tour that a user can interact with, where the system limits the maximum time spent based on an a priori estimate of average user requirements.

terms.name: Interaction time
terms.definition: Interaction time refers to the maximum amount of time allowed for a user to interact with a point of interest. This time limit is established by estimating the amount of time an average user needs.

terms.name: Semi-interactive tour
terms.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a virtual tour designed with a specific limit on the time a user can spend interacting at various points.

terms.name: Duration of exposure
terms.definition: Duration of exposure is the total time a user spends experiencing the virtual tour. This duration can be optimized through specific paths and strategies.

terms.name: Optimum path
terms.definition: An optimum path is a designed route through a virtual tour that achieves a specific optimization goal, such as visiting all points of interest in minimum time or visiting the maximum number of points of interest within a fixed time.

terms.name: Cyber sickness
terms.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition whose prevalence can be optimized through controlling the duration of exposure during a virtual tour, as the two factors are directly related.

parts.objective: Model a virtual experience as a weighted graph to find an optimal travel path covering all points of interest

key_points.text: The virtual world is formulated as a weighted graph (G), where vertices (V) represent all Points of Interest (POIs) and weighted edges (E) connect them.
The weight assigned to an edge represents the Euclidean distance between the two connected POIs.
In a realistic environment, the graph does not need to be complete, meaning some pairs of POIs may not have a direct path.
The optimization problem is to find a path (P) in the graph G that covers all vertices while minimizing time and maintaining a realistic speed.

terms.name: Graph
terms.definition: Graph is a representation of the virtual world as a weighted graph consisting of a set of vertices and a set of edges. The vertices represent all the points of interest, and the edges represent the weighted paths between those points of interest.

terms.name: Graph theoretic formulation
terms.definition: A graph theoretic formulation involves modeling the virtual world and the problem of finding an optimal path as a specific graph structure using vertices and edges.

terms.name: Virtual world
terms.definition: The virtual world, in this context, is modeled as a weighted graph to analyze travel and point of interest coverage within the simulated environment.

terms.name: Vertex
terms.definition: A vertex (or node) represents a Point of Interest (POI) within the virtual world, serving as a location in the graph structure.

terms.name: Edge
terms.definition: An edge is a connection between two vertices (Points of Interest) and, in this model, is weighted to denote the distance between the two points.

terms.name: Edge weight
terms.definition: The edge weight is the value assigned to an edge, representing the distance or the cost of traveling along the path from one Point of Interest to another.

terms.name: Euclidean distance
terms.definition: Euclidean distance is the value used to determine the weight of an edge between a pair of vertices. It denotes the distance between two points of interest that are directly connected.

terms.name: Complete graph
terms.definition: A complete graph is a graph where every single vertex is directly connected to every other vertex in the set, a state that is not always true in realistic environments.

parts.objective: Derive the formula and calculate the total travel time between two nodes using natural walking speed

key_points.text: The initial step in the algorithm is calculating the time required to travel between two directly connected nodes at natural walking speed.
The total travel time integral is calculated by integrating dx divided by 2.1 times V_actual over the distance D.
V_actual (actual instantaneous walking speed) is represented by a complex expression involving step frequency (f_x) and user height (h).
After simplifying the integral using various mathematical methods, the travel time estimate tau_D simplifies to D/V_naught.
The computed travel time assumes the model of natural walking speed.

terms.name: Natural walking model
terms.definition: The natural walking model is the assumption used in the algorithm to determine the time required to travel from one point of interest (POI) to the next.

terms.name: Perceived instantaneous walking speed
terms.definition: Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain into the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed V act.

terms.name: Actual instantaneous walking speed
terms.definition: Actual instantaneous walking speed is the realistic walking speed of the user that can be represented by formulas involving the instantaneous step frequency and user height.

terms.name: Travel time estimate
terms.definition: The travel time estimate is the result computed for the time between a pair of directly connected vertices after performing various simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier series expansions on the integral.

parts.objective: Adapt the Traveling Salesman Problem to minimize travel time on a non-complete graph

key_points.text: The goal is to find a path that minimizes total travel time while ensuring all vertices of the graph are included in the path.
This optimization problem is a variation of the classical Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP).
Because the original graph may not be complete, there may not be a direct path connecting every pair of vertices.
To solve the problem, hypothetical edges are introduced between disconnected vertices, and their length is defined as the shortest path length between those vertices.
The final path obtained by the TSP solver must be modified by replacing the hypothetical edges with the actual shortest paths found in the original graph.

terms.name: Edge weight
terms.definition: The edge weight is the value assigned to an edge, representing the length or time required to traverse that segment. This value can be the Euclidean distance or the shortest path length between two vertices.

terms.name: Euclidean distance
terms.definition: Euclidean distance is the standard geometric distance between two points, which serves as the initial edge length or weight between two directly connected vertices.

terms.name: Travelling Salesman Problem
terms.definition: The classical Traveling Salesman Problem seeks the shortest possible path in a complete graph that visits every node exactly once and eventually returns to the starting node.

terms.name: Complete graph
terms.definition: A complete graph is a graph used in the Traveling Salesman Problem to determine the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node.

terms.name: Hamiltonian path
terms.definition: A Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes in a graph, ensuring that each node is visited exactly once.

terms.name: Hypothetical edge
terms.definition: A hypothetical edge is an introduced connection between two vertices that do not have a direct connection in the original graph, created specifically for computational purposes.

terms.name: Shortest path
terms.definition: The shortest path is the path between two vertices that has the minimum sum of edge weights, and this length defines the weight of a hypothetical edge between them.

terms.name: Modified edge weight
terms.definition: The modified edge weight is the new definition of weight between two nodes; it is the Euclidean distance if they are directly connected, or the shortest path length if they are not connected.

terms.name: Modified graph
terms.definition: The modified graph is a new graph structure that includes hypothetical edges, which are introduced to turn the original problem into an instance of the standard Traveling Salesman Problem.

terms.name: TSP solver
terms.definition: A TSP solver is a standard algorithm or method used to find the optimal path for the Traveling Salesman Problem after a custom graph has been adapted.

parts.objective: Convert an optimal path found using a TSP solver back into a valid path that corresponds to the original graph structure

key_points.text: The initial step involves creating a complete graph ($G''$) from the original graph ($G$) by calculating hypothetical edge lengths, replacing missing direct connections.
The edge weights in the modified complete graph must be replaced from Euclidean distance to the actual travel time between vertices.
The modified complete graph, where weights represent travel time, is then input into a standard Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) solver to obtain an optimal time and path ($P_{opt}$).
The final stage requires modifying the TSP output ($P_{opt}$) to $P_{dashed, opt}$ by replacing hypothetical edges with the actual shortest path from the original graph.

terms.name: Edge weight
terms.definition: An edge weight is a value representing the cost or measure associated with traversing a specific edge, which in this method is replaced by the time taken to travel between the connected vertices.

terms.name: Travel time
terms.definition: Travel time is the metric used to define the edge weights in the modified complete graph, representing the time required to move from one vertex to another.

terms.name: Euclidean distance
terms.definition: Euclidean distance is the initial distance measurement used as the edge weight in the graph, which is later replaced by the actual time required for travel during the optimization process.

terms.name: TSP solver
terms.definition: A TSP solver is a standard algorithm used to take the modified graph as input and produce the optimal time and path that minimizes the total travel time.

parts.objective: Identify the limitation of minimum-time path algorithms regarding exceeding the cybersickness time threshold in large virtual environments

key_points.text: A minimum time calculation for an optimal path may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold if the virtual environment is very large.
VR experience optimization for cybersickness can be achieved by either minimizing the time to cover all points of interest or maximizing points covered within a given time threshold.

terms.name: Cybersickness time threshold
terms.definition: The cybersickness time threshold is the duration limit beyond which there is a possibility of the user experiencing cybersickness.

terms.name: Cybersickness
terms.definition: Cybersickness is a factor in virtual experience optimization that needs to be minimized, as the time spent in the virtual world can cross a threshold that creates a possibility of this condition.

terms.name: Natural walking speed
terms.definition: Natural walking speed is a parameter that was discussed and modeled as part of optimizing the virtual experience.

terms.name: Point of interest
terms.definition: Points of interest are the locations in the virtual world that are modeled as nodes in the graph and which must be covered during the minimum duration travel.
